quote: Amulius, having expelled his brother, seizes the kingdom; he adds crime to crime, murders his brother's male issue
notes: Alban usurpation preceding Rome's foundation; Rhea Silvia forced into Vestal virginity to cut off heirs.

quote: Thus a plot is concerted for the king on all sides.
notes: Coordinated two-pronged attack; the king is killed at the chapter's end ('and so they kill the king').

quote: an approving shout, following from all the people present, ratified to him both that title and the sovereignty
notes: Violent coup retroactively legitimated by popular assembly acclamation.

quote: there Remus fell from a blow received in the crowd.
notes: Augural dispute over the new city's kingship turns to bloodshed; Livy gives the wall-leaping variant as 'a more common account'.

quote: he gave them a code of laws
notes: First legal code plus the insignia of authority (twelve lictors) to make it respected.

quote: he opened as a sanctuary, a place which is now enclosed as you go down to the two groves.
notes: Population-building instrument: indiscriminate admission of fugitives, 'the first accession of strength'.

quote: He creates one hundred senators, either because that number was sufficient, or because there were only one hundred who could name their fathers.
notes: Origin of the senate and the patriciate.

quote: according to concert a tumult began, and upon a signal given the Roman youth ran different ways to carry off the virgins by force.
notes: State-orchestrated mass abduction under cover of a festival, after neighboring states refused intermarriage rights; demographic policy by force.

quote: Colonies were sent to both places, but more were found to give in their names for Crustuminum, because of the fertility of the soil.
notes: Earliest colony-enrollment preference datum in Livy: soil fertility drives differential volunteering — compare the Antium under-enrollment at III.1.

quote: Tatius bribes his maiden daughter with gold, to admit armed soldiers into the citadel
notes: Bribery of the commander's daughter betrays the citadel; the traitor killed by the bribers themselves.

quote: they not only conclude a peace, but form one state out of two. They associate the regal power, and transfer the entire sovereignty to Rome.
notes: The Sabine women's intervention converts a battle into a constitutional merger with dual kingship.

quote: At the same time three centuries of knights were enrolled, called Ramnenses, from Romulus; Tatienses, from Titus Tatius.
notes: Thirty curiae named for the Sabine women plus the three original equestrian centuries.

quote: he is slain at Lavinium, in a tumult which arose on his going thither to an anniversary sacrifice.
notes: Tatius shielded kinsmen from law-of-nations redress sought by the Laurentes; the denied legal remedy ends in his lynching; Romulus declines war and renews the treaty (ordinary aftermath).

quote: he kept three hundred of them armed as a body-guard not only in war but in peace, whom he called Celeres.
notes: Standing armed bodyguard in peacetime — an institution Livy links to Romulus being dearer to people and soldiers than to the fathers.

quote: some, who silently surmised that the king had been torn in pieces by the hands of the fathers
notes: Livy reports the senatorial-murder rumor and its suppression by the apotheosis story (Proculus Julius); coded low because Livy himself discounts it.

quote: the people began to murmur, that their slavery was multiplied, and that they had got a hundred sovereigns instead of one
notes: Succession dispute between the orders and ethnic blocs; resolved by the senate conceding popular election subject to patrum auctoritas.

quote: Thus the hundred senators divide the government among them, ten decuries being formed, and one selected from each decury
notes: The interregnum: rotating five-day supreme office; plus the compromise rule that popular election requires senate ratification.

quote: he divides the year into twelve months, according to the course of the moon
notes: Calendar reform, intercalation, dies fasti/nefasti, and the Janus temple as a war/peace indicator; Livy explicitly frames religion as an instrument of mass governance.

quote: He also selected virgins for Vesta, a priesthood derived from Alba, and not foreign to the family of the founder.
notes: Flamens, Vestals (with salaries from the public treasury), Salii, and the pontiff receiving a written, sealed system of rites — a documentary religious administration.

quote: Accordingly the matter was contested by appeal to the people.
notes: Perduellio procedure: duumvirs condemn, provocatio to the people, acquittal moved by the father's plea; expiation at public charge — the foundational appeal precedent.

quote: two chariots drawn by four horses being brought, he ties Mettus extended at full length to their carriages
notes: Allied dictator executed without trial for battlefield treachery; Livy marks it as the first and last punishment regardless of the laws of humanity.

quote: the Roman soldiery level all the public and private edifices indiscriminately to the ground
notes: Destruction of Alba and forced population transfer to Rome; temples spared by royal order.

quote: The leading persons among the Albans he enrols among the patricians
notes: Elite incorporation, new senate-house (Curia Hostilia), ten new cavalry troops from Albans — conquest converted to institutional absorption.

quote: he borrowed from an ancient nation, the Aequicolae, the form which the heralds still preserve, according to which restitution is demanded.
notes: Fetial procedure for declaring war: ritualized demand for restitution, thirty-three day term, senate consultation — a legal-religious protocol for external violence.

quote: a prison is built in the heart of the city, overlooking the forum, to intimidate the growing licentiousness.
notes: Carcer built explicitly as a deterrent response to population growth and 'clandestine crimes'.

quote: the city of Ostia built at the mouth of the Tiber; salt-pits were formed around it
notes: Port foundation with attached salt works — commercial-strategic settlement rather than agrarian safety valve.

quote: He is said to have been the first who earnestly sued for the crown, and to have made a set speech for the purpose of gaining the affections of the people
notes: First electoral canvassing at Rome; rivals (Ancus's sons) sent away hunting on election day — manipulation within ordinary forms.

quote: he elected a hundred into the fathers, who from that time were called Minorum Gentium
notes: Senate packing: a hundred new senators forming 'a party hearty in the king's cause' — institutional expansion as partisan instrument.

quote: Attus Navius, at that time a celebrated soothsayer, insisted that no alteration or new appointment of that kind could be made, unless the birds approved of it.
notes: Augural obstruction of the king's cavalry reform; king yields on form (no new-named centuries, only doubling) — religious veto power over institutional change; coded veto-deadlock by analogy.

quote: They determine therefore to prevent that disgrace by the sword.
notes: Succession grievance (guardian usurped their inheritance; a 'slave' next in line) motivates regicide plot via staged quarrel.

quote: the other, raising up his axe, struck it into his head, and leaving the weapon in the wound, they both rush out of the house.
notes: Regicide by hired rustics posing as litigants seeking the king's justice — the judicial audience as assassination vector.

quote: took possession of the kingdom by the consent of the senate, being the first who did so without the orders of the people.
notes: Managed succession: death concealed, regency performed from the palace window, senate consent without popular vote — Livy flags the procedural novelty.

quote: For he instituted the census, a most salutary measure for an empire destined to become so great
notes: Census, timocratic classes and centuries (I.43: voting order ensured 'the whole power might reside in the chief men of the state'); completed I.44 with 80,000 rated citizens under penalty of imprisonment and death for non-registration.

quote: having first secured their good will by dividing among them, man by man, the lands taken from their enemies, he ventured to propose the question to the people, whether they chose and ordered that he should be king
notes: Conquered land distributed viritim to buy a popular confirmation plebiscite; Livy's narrative at I.47 has Tarquin charge the land was taken 'from the leading men of the state' — distribution, not agitation, but the land-for-legitimacy exchange is explicit.

quote: Aruns Tarquinius and the younger Tullia, when they had, by immediate successive deaths, made their houses vacant for new nuptials, are united in marriage
notes: Double spousal murder clearing the way for the coup partnership; Servius 'rather not prohibiting than approving'.

quote: he rushed into the forum, accompanied by a party of armed men; then, whilst all were struck with dismay, seating himself on the throne before the senate-house
notes: Coup prepared by canvassing the minorum gentium senators and gifts to young men; his indictment of Servius centers on the land division and the census as class warfare.

quote: is slain by those who had been sent by Tarquin, and had overtaken him in his flight.
notes: King thrown down the senate-house steps, then murdered in the street; Tullia drives over the body — with him, Livy says, 'perished all just and legitimate reigns'.

quote: He put to death the principal senators, whom he suspected of having been in the interest of Servius.
notes: Purge plus structural tyranny: sole capital jurisdiction without assessors, senate left unfilled and unconsulted, armed bodyguard, rule 'by domestic counsels' — Livy's checklist of subverted institutions.

quote: he accomplished the ruin of this innocent man by bringing a false accusation against him.
notes: Judicial murder by planted evidence (bribed servant, smuggled swords) at the Latin council; condemned without defense and drowned — trial forms used as assassination instrument.

quote: he put to death the most eminent men of the city, accusing some of them to the people
notes: The poppy-heads stratagem: elite decapitation at Gabii with confiscated estates 'publicly distributed' to purchase acquiescence — largesse funded by proscription.

quote: he sent colonists to Signia and Circeii, to serve as defensive barriers hereafter to the city by land and sea.
notes: Colonies as population management: Livy says the king also considered the idle multitude 'a burden to the city' — settlement as labor-surplus disposal.

quote: they all take the oath as they were directed, and converting their sorrow into rage, follow Brutus as their leader
notes: The oath over Lucretia's body converts private outrage into a political compact to abolish the monarchy.

quote: he persuaded the multitude, already incensed, to deprive the king of his authority, and to order the banishment of L. Tarquin with his wife and children.
notes: Armed insurrection channeled through quasi-legal forms: Brutus convenes the assembly as tribune of the Celeres; grievance catalogue includes forced labor on the sewers ('instead of warriors had become labourers and stone-cutters').

quote: Two consuls, viz. Lucius Junius Brutus and Lucius Tarquinius Collatinus, were elected by the prefect of the city at the comitia by centuries
notes: Republican dual magistracy created by election in the Servian centuriate assembly 'according to the commentaries of Servius Tullius' — the revolution cites a written constitutional source.

quote: the origin of liberty you may date from this period, rather because the consular authority was made annual
notes: Foundation of the annual consulship; oath against kings also administered.

quote: he filled up the number of the senators, diminished by the king's murders, to the amount of three hundred
notes: Senate brought to 300 with equestrian conscripti; Livy credits this with concord between orders.

quote: he resigned his consulship; and removing all his effects to Lavinium, he withdrew from the state
notes: Consul forced out for bearing the Tarquin name; family banished by decree — political exclusion by name, resolved without violence.

quote: The letters, given to be a pledge of their sincerity, discovered the plot
notes: Aristocratic youth conspire to restore the Tarquins; detected by a slave informer who waited for documentary proof; spans II.3-4.

quote: After plundering the tyrants' effects, the traitors were condemned and capital punishment inflicted
notes: Judicial execution including the consul's own sons; informer slave rewarded with treasury money, liberty and citizenship (first vindicta manumission).

quote: Report represented that he aspired to the crown, because he had not substituted a colleague in the room of Brutus
notes: Regnum suspicion against sole consul defused by symbolic submission (fasces lowered) and demolition of his own house on the Velia.

quote: the laws regarding an appeal to the people against the magistrates, and that devoting the life and property of any one who should form a design of assuming regal authority
notes: Provocatio (appeal) law and sacratio against aspirants to kingship — the due-process constraint later cited in the Maelius affair (IV.13).

quote: Their attention, in the first place, was directed to the markets, and persons were sent, some to the Volscians, others to Cumae, to buy up corn
notes: Precautionary provisioning before Porsena's siege; salt monopoly taken into public hands, port-duties and taxes lifted from the poor — explicit concessions to keep plebs from accepting the Tarquins.

quote: Nevertheless the blockade continued, and there was a scarcity of corn, with a very high price
notes: Siege scarcity with price datum (qualitative); context for the Mucius Scaevola mission.

quote: fled from Regillum to Rome, accompanied by a great number of clients. The rights of citizenship and land on the other side of the Anio were conferred on them
notes: Mass client migration rewarded with citizenship, land, and a new tribe (the old Claudian); patron elevated to the senate.

quote: mention was made for the first time of nominating a dictator
notes: First creation of the dictatorship; Livy notes source uncertainty about year and first holder, and the office's terror effect: no appeal, no colleague.

quote: The same year the colony which king Tarquin had sent to Signia was recruited by filling up the number of the colonists
notes: Replenishment of a royal-era colony; same chapter notes onset of patrician oppression after Tarquin's death removed the external threat.

quote: The tribes at Rome were increased to twenty-one
notes: Administrative reorganization of the tribal structure.

actors: consuls P. Servilius and Ap. Claudius
quote: Those who were confined for debt, and those who were now at their liberty, hurry into the streets from all quarters and implore the protection of the people
notes: The centurion's display of scars and stripes ignites a city-wide debt protest; senate paralyzed, consuls split (Appius: coercion; Servilius: concession).

quote: They encouraged one another not to enrol their names, that it was better that all should perish together, than that they should perish alone
notes: Plebs welcome the Volscian attack as leverage and refuse enrollment until debt relief.

quote: He gave additional confidence to the assembly by an edict
notes: Wartime edict suspends debt detention and asset seizure for enrolled soldiers and their families; debtors enlist en masse — relief conditional on service.

quote: All was managed by violence, and the entire dread and danger with respect to personal liberty, was transferred from the debtors to the creditors
notes: After victory, Appius resumes harsh debt judgments; crowds forcibly prevent enforcement; levy for Sabine war collapses — reversal of coercive capacity.

quote: The people gave the dedication of the temple to M. Laetorius, the centurion of the first legion
notes: People assign a consular honor to a centurion explicitly to affront the consuls — symbolic power contest through a religious commission.

quote: held nightly meetings, some of them upon the Esquiline, and others upon the Aventine hill
notes: Plebeian counter-organization outside public institutions ('a thousand senate-houses and assemblies'); senate demands consular repression.

actors: consuls A. Virginius and T. Vetusius
quote: the consuls ascend the tribunal and summon the young men by name. But none of them made any answer
notes: Nominal summons publicly defied; crowd states terms: liberty first, arms after.

quote: the riot was quelled by the interposition of the consuls, in which however, without stones or weapons, there was more noise and angry words than mischief done
notes: Attempted exemplary arrest fails; in the senate three remedies debated (targeted relief / general relief / dictatorship without appeal).

quote: They choose Manius Valerius, son of Volesus, dictator
notes: Moderate dictator chosen over Appius precisely because trusted by plebs (brother's appeal law); edict mirrors Servilius's; ten legions raised — trust unlocks mobilization.

quote: colonists were sent from the city to Velitrae, and a colony planted there
notes: Conquered Volscian land colonized after the dictator's victory.

quote: Then quitting the senate-house, he abdicated his dictatorship
notes: Senate (swayed by money-lenders) rejects the dictator's debt-relief motion; he resigns in protest — promised relief defaulted on for the second time.

quote: retired, without the orders of the consuls, to the sacred mount, beyond the river Anio, three miles from the city
notes: First secession: army withdraws collectively after being held under oath; resolved by negotiation (Menenius's belly fable) leading to the tribunate. Livy notes the variant (Piso: Aventine).

quote: Thus two tribunes of the commons were created, Caius Licinius and L. Albinus
notes: Settlement terms of the secession: inviolable plebeian magistrates with auxilium against consuls; patricians excluded from the office. Livy flags source variants on number.

actors: consuls T. Geganius and P. Minutius
quote: first a scarcity of provisions, in consequence of the lands lying untilled during the secession of the commons
notes: Famine caused by the secession itself; three-route emergency procurement (Etruria, Cumae — ships seized by Aristodemus, Sicily); Etruscan grain via Tiber sustains the plebs.

quote: the Romans both augmented the number of their colonists at Velitrae, and despatched a new colony to the mountains of Norba
notes: Strategic colonization during the Volscian pestilence window.

quote: a great quantity of corn was imported from Sicily, and it was debated in the senate at what rate it should be given to the commons
notes: Senate price debate over state grain; Coriolanus proposes using hunger to roll back the tribunate; Livy appends his own counterfactual that the trade might have worked.

quote: Being condemned in his absence, he went into exile to the Volsci, threatening his country
notes: Near-lynching averted by tribunician trial date; patrician client-network counter-mobilization fails; condemned in absentia — the pilot Case A pivot event.

quote: having pitched his camp at the Cluilian trenches five miles from the city, he from thence ravages the Roman territory
notes: Exiled citizen leads foreign army on Rome, sparing patrician lands to sow discord; state embassies and priests fail; resolved extra-institutionally by his mother's supplication (II.40).

quote: Then, for the first time, the Agrarian law was proposed, which even down to our own recollection was never agitated without the greatest commotions in the state
notes: Cassius's bill: Hernican land + occupied public land, with Latin allies included; defeated by consular opposition and plebeian suspicion of regnum — the founding event of Case C.

actors: quaestors Kaeso Fabius and L. Valerius (one tradition)
quote: As soon as he went out of office, it is certain that he was condemned and put to death
notes: Execution after office; Livy preserves two trial traditions (domestic vs quaestorian perduellio) and prefers the public one; house demolished, property consecrated to Ceres with inscribed statue.

quote: In that year also the minds of the people were excited by the charms of the agrarian law
notes: Agitation resumes once the proposer is dead; aggravated by consul selling war booty to the treasury instead of distributing it.

quote: had taken on him the task of obstructing the military preparations
notes: Tribune blocks the levy to force the agrarian law; defeated when his own colleagues side with the consuls — first instance of the tribune-vs-tribune tactic Machiavelli catalogues in I.37.

quote: the infantry refused to pursue them when routed
notes: Army deliberately withholds victory out of hatred of the consul; returns to camp without orders — political insubordination inside the military instrument.

quote: It was Titus Pontificius: he pursuing the same course, as if it had succeeded with Sp. Licinius, obstructed the levy for a little time
notes: Appius's doctrine: co-opt some tribunes to veto their colleague — 'four tribunes against one' completes the levy; the institutionalization of divide-the-college.

actors: consuls M. Fabius and Cn. Manlius
quote: The Roman consuls also dreaded nothing else, than their own strength, and their own arms
notes: Consuls refuse battle fearing politically disaffected troops; soldiers demand battle and are bound by voluntary oath to return victorious — loyalty crisis resolved by religious self-binding.

quote: that they should distribute among the commons the land taken from the enemy in as equal a proportion as possible
notes: A patrician consul proposes preemptive distribution of conquered land; rejected with scorn by his own order — elite refusal of the cheap concession.

quote: That war, as the property of our family, it is our determination to conduct at our own private expense
notes: A public war privatized to a single clan (306 Fabii to the Cremera, II.49-50, annihilated) — the gens as military contractor; precedent-setting fusion of private force and public war.

actors: tribunes Q. Considius and T. Genucius
quote: the loss of the fort of Cremera, whilst the consul had his standing camp at no great distance from thence, was the charge against him
notes: Tribunician prosecution of an ex-consul for military failure; fined 2,000 asses; dies of the disgrace — the fine datum is one of the few quantitative values in the book.

actors: tribunes L. Caedicius and T. Statius
quote: Another senator, Sp. Servilius, being soon after arraigned, as soon as he went out of office
notes: Second tribunician prosecution; defendant defends boldly rather than supplicating and survives — paired contrast case to Menenius within one chapter.

quote: bring word that he was found dead in his house
notes: Tribune prosecuting ex-consuls found dead on trial morning; Livy: patricians openly wished to be credited with it; tribunes intimidated, levy proceeds — assassination as deterrent (cf. Disc I.44 context).

quote: the lictors being maltreated, the fasces broken, they are driven from the forum into the senate-house
notes: Ex-centurion resists enrollment as common soldier, appeals to the people when tribunes fail him; crowd breaks consular enforcement — physical defeat of magistracy.

quote: the contest would have ended in a battle, not without blood, had not Quintius, the other consul
notes: Showdown over the Publilian law (tribal election of tribunes); tribune and consul exchange arrest orders; defused by the moderate consul — near-civil-violence over an electoral rule.

quote: Then for the first time the tribunes were elected in the comitia by tribes
notes: Publilian law carried: removes patrician client-vote influence over tribunician elections (Piso: college raised to five); structural de-patronization of the office.

quote: For they were not only unwilling to conquer, like Fabius' army, but they wished to be conquered
notes: Army deliberately loses to spite the consul; Appius responds with beatings, beheadings, and decimation ('every tenth man was drawn by lot for punishment') — maximal coercion after political alienation.

actors: tribunes M. Duilius and C. Sicinius
quote: Never before was an accused person so hateful to the commons brought to trial before the people
notes: Trial of the chief opponent of the agrarian law; defendant refuses supplication, intimidates the court; dies before the adjourned trial day (variant: suicide per Dionysius).

actors: consuls T. Numicius Priscus and A. Virginius
quote: The commons appeared determined no longer to brook a delay of the agrarian law, and extreme violence was on the eve of being resorted to
notes: Sedition on the point of breaking out; checked only by Volscian incursion — external war as safety valve (the 'trarre fuora uno esercito' tactic observed in the wild).

actors: consuls T. Quintius and Q. Servilius
quote: The exasperated commons refused to attend the consular elections
notes: Electoral abstention as protest; consuls elected by patricians and their dependents alone — participation withdrawal as a channel of conflict.

quote: both the abettors of the agrarian law had raised themselves to the hope of carrying the measure
notes: Agrarian law pushed with one consul's support; defused by Fabius's Antium colony compromise.

actors: triumvirs T. Quintius, A. Virginius, P. Furius
quote: so few gave in their names that Volscian colonists were added to fill up the number
notes: Colony to Antium as agrarian safety valve; Roman under-enrollment, quota filled with Volscians.

quote: when it was announced to the senate that a defection was intended, the consuls were charged to inquire into the business
notes: Suspected defection of the Antium colony; leaders summoned and interrogated, dismissed under suspicion.

quote: he would propose a law, that five persons be appointed to draw up laws regarding the consular power
notes: Terentilian rogation to codify/limit consular power; deferred under patrician pressure, recurs for years.

quote: A triumph was by universal consent due to the consul: but the matter was deferred, the tribune still pressing his law
notes: Tribune links triumph grant to the law; eventually yields and triumph is held.

quote: Whomsoever the lictor laid hold of by order of the consul, him the tribune ordered to be discharged
notes: Mutual obstruction: tribunes block the levy, consuls block the law; escalates to force.

quote: Under his guidance the tribunes were frequently driven from the forum, the commons routed and dispersed
notes: Patrician strong-arm disruption of assemblies led by Caeso; triggers his prosecution.

quote: Being discharged from the forum, he went the following night into exile among the Etrurians
notes: Trial spans 3:11-13; first use of public bail (ten sureties of 3,000 asses); Caeso flees, fine exacted ruinously from his father Cincinnatus.

quote: The exiles and slaves to the number of four thousand and five hundred men took possession of the Capitol and citadel during the night
notes: Armed seizure of the Capitol; recaptured by assault with Tusculan aid (3:18), consul P. Valerius killed; Herdonius slain.

quote: the law, however, could neither be prepared, nor could the consul proceed to the Capitol
notes: Tribunes press the Terentilian law during the Capitol occupation; consul refuses arms-down lawmaking; standoff broken only by nightfall.

quote: by the most zealous exertions of the patricians, Lucius Quintius Cincinnatus, Caeso's father, is elected consul to enter on his office without delay
notes: Partisan suffect election of Caeso's father, to plebeian dismay.

quote: The tribunes then began to cavil, and wished to absolve the people from their obligation
notes: Consul bypasses levy obstruction via the soldiers' prior oath; threatens dictatorship and out-of-city assembly beyond appeal.

quote: the tribunes were re-appointed notwithstanding the remonstrances of the consuls
notes: Senate decrees against continuing magistracies; tribunes re-elected anyway; Quintius refuses his own re-election.

quote: appoint a day of trial for Marcus Volscius, because he had come forward as a manifestly false witness against Caeso
notes: Quaestorian prosecution of the false witness; tribunes obstruct for years; condemned and exiled to Lanuvium in 3:29 under the dictator's shadow.

quote: The tribunes, according to their practice, attempted to obstruct the levy
notes: Obstruction overtaken by the Sabine incursion panic; commons then enlist willingly (3:26).

quote: they were determined that a dictator should be appointed to retrieve their embarrassed affairs
notes: Cincinnatus taken from the plough; rescues Minucius's besieged army at Algidum, forces Minucius to resign consulship, triumphs, resigns on day 16 (3:26-29).

quote: The commons succeeded in electing the same tribunes for the fifth time
notes: Continuation of tribunician office against patrician resistance; patricians block the law while armies are afield.

quote: On the thirty-sixth year after the first tribunes, ten were elected, two from each class
notes: Tribunate enlarged to ten as the price of allowing the levy; condition that the same men not be re-elected.

quote: They were both condemned, to the great mortification of the patricians; Romilius to pay ten thousand asses; Veturius, fifteen thousand
notes: Ex-consuls fined for selling the army's booty to refill the treasury; fiscal grievance of the soldiers prosecuted politically.

quote: A law was proposed regarding the making Mount Aventine public property
notes: Icilian law on the Aventine (urban land for the plebs); preserved as a condition in the decemvirate bargain (3:32).

quote: It was resolved that decemvirs should be elected without appeal, and that there should be no other magistrate during that year
notes: After the Athens embassy, all ordinary magistracies suspended in favor of a law-writing college without appeal; plebeian admission bargained away for the Icilian/devoting laws.

quote: Caius Julius, a decemvir, appointed a day of trial for Sestius, and appeared before the people as prosecutor
notes: Decemvir voluntarily cedes his unappealable jurisdiction to the people — Livy's exhibit of first-college moderation.

quote: the laws of the ten tables were passed at the assembly voting by centuries
notes: Ten Tables published for public comment then enacted; two more tables felt wanting, motivating a second college.

quote: he appoints as decemvirs men by no means equal in rank of life: himself in the first instance
notes: Appius, presiding over the election meant to exclude him, returns himself and a slate of dependents for the second decemvirate.

quote: they all suddenly came forth with the twelve fasces. One hundred and twenty lictors filled the forum
notes: Second college drops collegial rotation, displays full coercive apparatus, rules by terror; mutual non-interference pact, no comitia planned.

quote: No new election of magistrates having taken place, private persons came forth as decemvirs
notes: Decemvirs hold power past their term without election; senate finally convened under war pressure; Valerius and Horatius dissent (3:39-41).

quote: lest any enterprise should succeed under the conduct and auspices of the decemvirs, suffered themselves to be beaten, to their own disgrace
notes: Passive mutiny: armies let themselves be defeated at Eretum and Algidum rather than win for the decemvirs.

quote: instructions were given to the soldiers whom they had sent to accompany him in that expedition, to attack him in a convenient place and slay him
notes: State-ordered assassination of the soldier agitating for tribunate restoration and secession; cover story unravels at the burial detail.

quote: He then transfixes the girl's breast, and looking back towards the tribunal, he says, With this blood I devote thee, Appius, and thy head
notes: Spans 3:44-48: fraudulent enslavement claim engineered by Appius; father kills daughter to prevent her seizure — the trigger of the decemvirate's fall.

quote: The decemvir's lictor attacks Valerius and Horatius: the fasces are broken by the people
notes: Crowd breaks decemviral coercion in the forum; Appius flees with covered head; Oppius convenes the senate.

quote: there was a general cry to arms, they snatched up their standards, and set out for Rome
notes: Virginius's appeal turns the army; it marches to Rome and occupies the Aventine, electing ten military tribunes (3:51); Sabine-front army follows under Icilius and Numitorius.

quote: passes from the Aventine to the Sacred mount; Duilius affirming that serious concern for business would not enter the minds of the patricians
notes: Second secession to the Sacred Mount; whole plebs follows; negotiated through Valerius and Horatius on terms of tribunate, appeal, and amnesty (3:53).

quote: the decemvirs come forth into the assembly, and resign their office, to the great joy of all
notes: Senate decree ends the decemvirate; pontifex maximus holds the election restoring the tribunate; Icilian amnesty plebiscite and Duilian law for consuls with appeal follow in the same chapter.

quote: they proposed a law in the assembly of the centuries, that whatever the commons ordered collectively, should bind the entire people
notes: Valerio-Horatian package: plebiscites binding, appeal guaranteed against magistracies created without it, tribunician sacrosanctity renewed, senate decrees archived with plebeian aediles at Ceres.

quote: still he both appealed to the tribunes, and, when no one regarded him, being seized by the bailiff, he exclaims, I appeal
notes: The abolisher of appeal appeals; imprisoned pending trial on the single charge of adjudging a free person to slavery; C. Claudius intercedes in vain (3:58).

quote: Oppius was also thrown into prison, where he put a period to his life before the day of trial
notes: Appius and Oppius die in prison before trial (suicides); their property confiscated by the tribunes; the other decemvirs exiled with property confiscated; claimant M. Claudius condemned, spared death, exiled to Tibur.

quote: Then for the first time a triumph was celebrated by order of the people, without the authority of the senate
notes: Senate refuses the victorious consuls a triumph; Icilius carries it through the tribes — a constitutional precedent transferring an honors decision to the people.

quote: a conspiracy being formed among the tribunes to have the same tribunes re-elected
notes: Duilius blocks the self-continuation scheme of his colleagues, accepting five elected tribunes who co-opt the rest under the law's letter.

quote: carried a proposal, that whoever took the votes of the commons in electing tribunes of the people, he should go on taking the votes, until he elected ten tribunes of the people
notes: Trebonian law closes the co-optation loophole after patricians slipped two consulars into the college.

quote: Acts of injustice began to be committed by the younger patricians on the commons when perfectly quiet
notes: Low-level violence against commons and even tribunes in the magistracy's weak months; tribunate felt as 'mere names'.

quote: the levy proclaimed two years previously could not be proceeded with, the commons now refusing obedience
notes: Two-year levy paralysis invites enemy raids to Rome's gates; resolved by Quintius's speech — 'By universal consent the levy is decreed and held' (3:69).

quote: The tribes, when convened, decided that the district was the public property of the Roman people
notes: Rome, chosen as arbitrator between Aricia and Ardea, votes the disputed land to itself on Scaptius's urging over consular and senatorial protest — a popular-assembly scandal over land.

actors: consuls M. Genucius and C. Curtius
quote: that they never should hold a levee while he lived, before the commons had first ratified the laws proposed by him and his colleagues
notes: Canuleius blocks the levy to force the intermarriage law and plebeian-consulship bill; patricians had welcomed war rumors to suspend tribunician proceedings.

quote: the patricians, being at length overpowered, agreed that the law regarding intermarriage should be passed
notes: Repeal of the decemviral intermarriage ban (lex Canuleia), conceded to divert the plebeian-consulship demand; spans chs. 1-6.

quote: they suffered tribunes of the soldiers with consular authority to be elected from the patricians and commons without distinction
notes: Compromise creating military tribunes with consular power in place of opening the consulship; brokered in private meetings of leading men; first election returns all patricians.

quote: they resigned the honour, in pursuance of a decree of the augurs, as if unduly elected
notes: First consular tribunes forced to abdicate in month three over a flaw in the presiding magistrate's auspices; religious procedure as political instrument.

quote: The contest whether consuls or military tribunes should be elected, kept the matter for several days in a state of interregnum
notes: Patricians prevail; consuls elected; Livy cites the Ardean treaty and the linen books (Licinius Macer) for their names — documentary source note.

quote: This same year was the commencement of the censorship, a thing which arose from an humble origin
notes: Census backlog plus consular overload produces a dedicated registry magistracy; tribunes acquiesce seeing it as drudgery; administrative-records institution par excellence.

quote: The nobles called in the Romans to the relief of their besieged city; the commons called upon the Volscians to join them in storming Ardea
notes: Polity is Ardea, not Rome: marriage dispute escalates through factions to civil war with BOTH sides inviting foreign forces — the clearest external-appeal case in Book 4.

quote: beheading the principal authors of that commotion, and confiscating their effects to the public treasury of the Ardeans
notes: Roman consul executes the Ardean sedition leaders and confiscates property into Ardea's treasury; punitive confiscation procedure recorded.

quote: a colony should be sent thither as a protection against the Volscians
notes: Senate frames the colony publicly as defense while quietly restoring the disputed land to Ardea by enrolling more Rutulians than Romans; the stated record diverges from the intent (Livy says so).

quote: a day having been appointed for them by the tribunes to appear before the people, they escaped all vexatious annoyance by enrolling themselves as settlers and remaining in the colony
notes: Tribunician prosecution of land commissioners for assigning land to allies; defendants evade trial by joining the colony they founded.

quote: could neither prevail on the consuls to submit to the senate the questions concerning the division of the lands among the people
notes: Agrarian motion and levy threat both fail; his menace of blocking the levy was laughed at because no war impended.

quote: Their misfortunes began with famine; whether it was that the season was unfavourable to the crops, or that the cultivation of the land was relinquished
notes: Livy preserves two causal traditions (bad harvest vs fields deserted for city politics) without deciding; famine culminates in plebeian suicides in the Tiber.

quote: that Lucius Minutius should be appointed president of the market
notes: New emergency supply magistracy; administration by compulsory stock declaration, forced sale of surplus over a month's provision, halving of slave rations, prosecution of corn-hoarders — exposing rather than relieving the shortage.

quote: having, by the assistance of his friends and clients, bought up corn from Etruria at his private expense
notes: Private procurement through personal networks; Livy conjectures ('I think') it had impeded the public relief effort; largesses win a mass following and consular hopes.

quote: that arms were collecting in the house of Maelius, and that he held assemblies in his house: and that his designs were unquestionably bent on regal dominion
notes: Intelligence reaches Minucius because the same personnel frequented both grain operations; reported to the senate as a regnum plot with bribed tribunes and assigned roles.

quote: That there was wanting a man not only determined in himself, but one who was unshackled and freed from the fetters of those laws
notes: Explicit rationale: consuls are bound by the appeal (provocatio) laws, so an office above them is required; Cincinnatus past eighty accepts.

quote: Ahala Servilius overtook and slew him whilst exclaiming in this manner
notes: Killed without trial while resisting the dictator's summons; dictator ratifies ('iure caesum' speech ch.15: lawful even if innocent, for refusing the summons); goods sold by quaestors into treasury; house razed (Aequimelium, ch.16); confiscated grain distributed at one as per bushel by Minucius.

actors: tribunes Q. Caecilius, Q. Junius, Sex. Titinius
quote: They succeeded, therefore, in having an election hell for military tribunes rather than for consuls
notes: Tribunes exploit resentment at Maelius's death to force military-tribune elections; commons nonetheless elect only three, all patrician. Livy here refutes the 11th-tribune tradition against a false statue inscription.

actors: L. Quinctius Cincinnatus jr (master of horse)
quote: the senate, as in an alarming crisis, ordered Mamercus Aemilius to be appointed dictator
notes: War dictator against Veii/Fidenae after the murder of Roman ambassadors; routine military appointment.

quote: had both appointed a day of trial for Minucius, and had also proposed a law for confiscating the property of Servilius Ahala
notes: Retributive prosecution over the Maelius killing — charges that the victim was framed and killed uncondemned; Livy: the charges 'proved to be more idle than the author himself'.

quote: It is determined that Aulus Servilius be appointed dictator
notes: Enemy at the Colline gate during pestilence; named at night by consul Virginius with colleague's consent.

quote: the senate, apprehending a great attack threatening from that quarter, ordered Mamercus Aemilius again to be appointed dictator
notes: Pan-Etruscan threat after the fall of Fidenae; Livy flags conflicting magistrate lists for the year, both sides citing the linen books.

quote: That he would propose a law, that the censorship should not last longer than a year and half
notes: Term-limit law passed amid popular approval; the censors retaliate by degrading Mamercus from his tribe, taxing him eight-fold and disfranchising him; popular violence against the censors barely restrained — by Mamercus himself.

quote: The tribunes of the people, by preventing the election of consuls by incessant harangues, succeeded at length
notes: Consular elections blocked to the brink of interregnum; military tribunes elected — all patricians again.

quote: Apprehending a famine for the agriculturists, they sent into Etruria, and the Pomptine district, and to Cumae, and at last to Sicily also to procure corn
notes: Preemptive procurement during pestilence along the same four routes as the 492 crisis; 'nor was there any danger from a scarcity of corn, because provision had been previously made'.

quote: that no person be allowed to add white to his garment for the purposes of canvassing
notes: Anti-whitening (ambitus) law conceived in secret meetings at tribunes' houses to suppress patrician electioneering; senate counters by decreeing consular elections.

actors: consuls T. Quintius and C. Julius Mento
quote: the senate calls on you, that you would, by virtue of your authority, compel the consuls to nominate a dictator in so critical a conjuncture of the state
notes: Constitutional inversion: the senate invokes TRIBUNICIAN coercion (threat of imprisonment) against refusing consuls to force a dictator nomination; consuls prefer yielding to tribunes over the senate.

actors: consuls L. Papirius Crassus and L. Junius
quote: was about to be introduced by the tribunes, took the lead themselves in proposing it
notes: Law converting livestock fines to money appraisal; consuls preempt the tribunes to capture credit for a popular measure.

quote: The tribunes, by threatening that they would stop the levy, so far prevailed that the consuls should take the sense of the people concerning the war
notes: Levy threat converts a senate war decision into a popular vote (all centuries vote for the Veientian war); commons also extract military-tribune elections for the next year.

quote: they hated the tribunes, they insisted on a dictator, the hopes of the state now seemed to rest on him
notes: Third Mamercus dictatorship after the Veii defeat under divided tribune command; appointed despite his censorial disfranchisement — 'so little did censorial animadversion avail'; augural scruple about nomination resolved.

quote: a decree of the senate might be passed in the absence of the tribunes of the commons
notes: Senate decree for consular elections engineered while plebeian tribunes are out of the city, defeating candidacies premised on land distribution, colonies, and a property tax for soldiers' pay.

quote: is condemned in a fine of ten thousand asses in weight, of brass
notes: Trial of the defeated commanders of Veii; Postumius fined 10,000 asses, Quintius acquitted by all tribes on service record and his father Cincinnatus's memory; Tempanius's soldierly testimony declines to judge the consul.

quote: To Caius Sempronius I have nothing more to say, since when in office he has attained this good fortune, to be so dear to his soldiers
notes: Prosecution of the consul beaten in the Volscian campaign abandoned when his former soldiers, now tribunes, threaten to share his defendant's garb — soldier loyalty as judicial shield.

quote: an unexpected mass of dissensions arose between the commons and patricians, which commenced with doubling the number of quaestors
notes: Quaestors doubled to four with the compromise (after a blocked year and interregnum) that they be elected promiscuously from both orders; tribunes had obstructed patrician assemblies and interrex decrees.

quote: he, having pleaded his own cause with a spirit by no means subdued, is condemned in a fine of fifteen thousand asses
notes: Renewed prosecution driven by rage at plebeian defeats in the first open quaestor elections; Sempronius refuses to buy acquittal by dropping his opposition to land division.

quote: Postumia, a Vestal virgin, is tried for a breach of chastity, though guiltless of the charge
notes: Acquitted; pontiff orders restraint in dress and manner — a reputational-regulation verdict.

quote: The slaves conspire to set fire to the city in several quarters
notes: Arson-diversion plot to seize the citadel and Capitol; betrayed by two accomplices rewarded with 10,000 asses from the treasury and freedom — a priced informant market.

quote: Quintus Servilius Priscus was created dictator in pursuance of a decree of the senate
notes: After defeat caused by alternating-day command discord between tribunes at Algidum — the commander-plurality failure Livy editorializes on.

quote: the senate very opportunely voted in full assembly that a colony should be conducted to Lavici
notes: 1,500 colonists at two acres each, voted explicitly BEFORE the tribunes could raise agrarian agitation over the captured Lavican land — the colony-as-preemption tactic.

actors: tribunes Sp. Maecilius and Sp. Maetilius
quote: they had proposed a bill, that the land taken from the enemy should be divided man by man
notes: Universal distribution bill threatening confiscation of nobles' holdings; defeated by the hereditary Claudian tactic of buying colleague vetoes — six tribunes protest and the movers abandon the bill.

quote: was defeated by the protests of his colleagues, who declared openly that they would suffer no order of the commons to be passed, unless with the approbation of the senate
notes: Bolae colonization bill killed by co-opted vetoes; the sequel (Postumius's 'woe to my soldiers') detonates the mutiny of ch.50.

quote: their indignation burst forth to such a degree, that the military tribune was overwhelmed with stones by his own army
notes: Army lynches its commander after a broken plunder promise, the 'woe to my soldiers' threat, a stoned quaestor, and executions under the hurdle — military-mutiny escalating to killing.

quote: When the plebeian tribunes did not suffer the decree of the senate to pass, and when they also protested against the election of consuls, the affair was brought to an interregnum
notes: Murder-inquiry decree and consular elections both blocked; patricians win the interregnum; inquiry then entrusted to consuls by the commons themselves (ch.51), executed with lenity — a few culprits reportedly suicide.

actors: consuls A. Cornelius Cossus and L. Furius Medullinus
quote: an inquiry into the murder of Postumius, and that the commons should appoint whomsoever they thought proper to conduct the inquiry
notes: Commons voluntarily delegate the mutiny inquiry to the consuls; Livy contrasts the speed of punitive law with the dormancy of laws benefiting the commons, and notes the missed chance to pacify via Bolae land division.

quote: Marcus Maenius, a proposer of an agrarian law, would obstruct Valerius the consul when holding a levy
notes: Agrarian-leverage levy block broken when nine tribunes decree support for the consul against their colleague; a few resisters imprisoned, rest take the oath; consul then denies the army its booty (quaestors sell it into the treasury) and is mocked in ovation verses while Maenius is lionized — kept from office by switching to consular elections.

quote: avenged by then electing plebeians for the first time as quaestors
notes: First plebeians in a patrician magistracy (three of four places), engineered by the Icilii as revenge for being denied military-tribune elections; patricians lament honors 'lost, not shared'.

quote: Neither the consuls effected the levy, nor the tribunes the election which they desired
notes: Mutual blockade (levy vs elections) broken by the fall of Carventa; senate concedes military-tribune elections but bars sitting tribunes from candidacy and re-election — targeted at the Icilii.

actors: military tribunes C. Julius and P. Cornelius
quote: complaining fruitlessly that the military tribunes would not conform to the judgment of the senate, at last appealed even to the tribunes of the commons
notes: Magistrates refuse the senate's dictator order; patricians reduced to invoking tribunician power against their own; plebeian tribunes gleefully decline.

actors: C. Servilius Ahala (military tribune, then master of horse)
quote: he would, on the following night, nominate a dictator; and if any one protested against a decree of the senate being passed, that he would be content with its authority
notes: Ahala breaks his colleagues' refusal by nominating Cornelius on the senate's bare auctoritas; is made master of horse and re-elected — Livy's moral on unsought honors.

quote: they produced in the people an aversion to undertaking a war, the time for proposing the law was adjourned
notes: Tribunes frame the Veii declaration as patrician class war ('the war of the greatest moment was that between the patricians and commons'), parading veterans' scars; the war vote is postponed to avoid defeat.

quote: the senate should decree that the soldiers should receive pay out of the public treasury, whereas up to that period every one had discharged that duty at his own expense
notes: Institution of the stipendium, granted preemptively 'before any mention should be made of it by the commons or tribunes' — the largest fiscal-military innovation of the book, timed to defuse agitation before the Veii war.

quote: the tribunes publicly declared, that they would afford protection to any one who should refuse to contribute his proportion for the pay of the soldiers
notes: Tribunes identify the tax financing the stipendium as its hidden cost and offer protection to refusers; defeated by demonstrative voluntary contributions of weighed brass by senators and allied leading plebeians — emulation beats obstruction; Veii war then voted.

quote: they run forward into the assembly, stir up the minds of the commons, saying that this was the motive for which pay had been established for the soldiers
notes: Tribunician agitation against the unprecedented winter continuation of the Veii siege; countered by Appius Claudius's speech (5:3-6) and overtaken by patriotic reaction after the fire disaster (5:7).

quote: Then for the first time the cavalry began to serve on their own horses.
notes: After the Veii fire disaster, equestrians volunteer on their own horses and commons volunteer for service; senate institutes cavalry stipend — institutional innovation defusing the tribunician agitation of 5:2.

quote: I will immediately nominate a dictator, who will oblige them to retire from office
notes: Senate forces early resignation of the discredited military tribunes; plebeian tribunes threaten imprisonment; Ahala's dictator threat resolves it within institutional channels.

quote: The tribunes of the commons, by their seditious harangues, caused these things, grievous in themselves, to seem more exasperating
notes: Agitation against simultaneous levy (including seniors) and war tax to fund military pay; continues into the tax strike of 5:12.

quote: for the purpose of weakening the Trebonian law, it was managed that Caius Lacerius and Marcus Acutius should be admitted as tribunes of the commons
notes: Patrician-influenced co-optation of plebeian tribunes to undermine the Trebonian law; backlash led by Cn. Trebonius in 5:11.

actors: tribunes P. Curiatius, M. Metilius, M. Minucius
quote: the commons condemn the accused [in a fine] of ten thousand asses in weight
notes: Trial set in 5:11 by tribunes deflecting popular anger from the co-optation scandal onto the defeated commanders; condemned to a 10,000-as fine — command failure criminalized through ordinary channels.

quote: publish a form of an agrarian law, and prevent the tax from being contributed
notes: Tribunes convert the trial victory into a distributive program plus tax strike; army pay blocked and the camp nearly infected by the city's sedition; strike relaxed after the plebeian electoral breakthrough later in the chapter.

quote: the election of one of the commons, Publius Licinius Calvus, military tribune with consular power
notes: First plebeian elected military tribune with consular power — precedent-setting breakthrough; tribunes then relax the tax obstruction and the tax is paid.

quote: almost all the centuries appointed the other plebeian candidates as military tribunes with consular authority
notes: Following Licinius Calvus's moderate tenure, plebeians sweep the consular tribunate (only one patrician elected).

quote: the lectisternium being then for the first time introduced into the city of Rome for eight days
notes: Pestilence response via Sibylline books; first lectisternium; prisoners' chains removed during the rite — religious innovation with social effects.

quote: The people, overawed as well by the dignity of the candidates as by a sense of religion, elected all the military tribunes with consular power from among the patricians
notes: Patricians retake all consular-tribunate seats by coordinated candidacies plus religious framing of the pestilence as divine anger at mixed elections.

quote: having raised a body of men, not by a regular levy, (for they were prevented by the tribunes of the commons,) but [a body consisting] mostly of volunteers
notes: Tribunician veto blocks the regular levy against the Tarquinian raids; commanders improvise a volunteer force — formal obstruction circumvented informally.

actors: interreges L. Valerius, Q. Servilius Fidenas, M. Furius Camillus
quote: the tribunes of the commons impeding the elections until it was previously stipulated, that the greater number of the military tribunes should be elected out of the commons
notes: During the expiation-driven interregnum, tribunes blockade elections until a plebeian-majority stipulation is conceded.

quote: Marcus Furius Camillus, being nominated dictator, appointed Publius Cornelius Scipio his master of the horse
notes: Dictatorship for the final Veii campaign; levy proceeds with no one declining service — contrast with the obstructed levies before.

quote: What did they thinly should be done with respect to the spoil? Two opinions divided the senate
notes: TAXONOMY APPROXIMATION: dispute is over war BOOTY distribution, not grain — coded here as the nearest distributional-dispute type. Licinius's open-distribution proposal defeats Appius's treasury/pay plan; populace flocks to the camp. Sequels: tithe controversy (5:23, 5:25), Camillus's trial (5:32). OCR artifact 'thinly' (for 'think') is verbatim in the source text.

quote: they resolved that a colony should be sent off to the Volscian country, for which three thousand Roman citizens should be enrolled
notes: Colony voted explicitly to assuage multiplying sedition; allotments of 3 7/12 iugera scorned as a sop against the greater hope of Veientian land — enrollment quota and allotment size recorded.

quote: Nay, even that scheme was proposed, which after the taking of Rome by the Gauls was still more strongly urged, of removing to Veii
notes: Proposal to relocate half the commons and half the senate to Veii; patricians declare they will die before voting it; continues to 5:30.

quote: whenever a clamour was set up for the purpose of commencing a riot, the principal members of the senate, presenting themselves among the foremost to the crowd
notes: Near-riot over the migration bill checked without force: senators offer their own persons and the crowd's respect for age and rank restrains violence — an 'ordinary' resolution by pure status authority.

quote: Which annoyance the patricians avenged by passing a decree of the senate that consuls should be elected, magistrates detested by the commons
notes: After the commons re-elect pro-law tribunes, the senate retaliates by restoring consular elections after a fifteen-year interval.

quote: by a most pernicious precedent these men, though innocent, were condemned [to pay a fine of] ten thousand asses in weight
notes: Ex-tribunes prosecuted solely for having vetoed the migration law in the patrician interest; Livy and Camillus both flag the precedent as destroying the independence of the veto.

quote: a decree of the senate was passed, that seven acres a man of Veientian territory should be distributed to the commons
notes: Migration-to-Veii law defeated by one tribe after patrician supplication campaign; next day the senate concedes a 7-iugera viritane distribution of Veientian land including all free household members — rejection paired with a quantified concession.

quote: on a day [of trial] being appointed for him by Lucius Appuleius, a tribune of the people, in reference to the Veientian spoil
notes: Camillus, canvassing his clients, hears they will pay his fine but not acquit; withdraws to exile at Ardea; fined 15,000 asses in absence — the spoils controversy criminalized its own victorious general.

quote: Aruns, a native of Clusium, introduced wine into Gaul for the purpose of enticing the nation, through resentment for his wife's having been debauched by Lucumo
notes: Private injury without civic remedy leads to invitation of foreign force; Livy himself doubts the tale's chronology (Gauls crossed 200 years earlier). NOTE: Livy has Aruns's WIFE debauched by Lucumo; Machiavelli Disc I.7 renders it as Arruns's SISTER — a variant recorded in alignment aln:a-chiusi-addition.

quote: those persons, whose punishment was under consideration, were elected military tribunes with consular power for the ensuing year
notes: Senate privately agrees the Gauls' demand for surrender of the law-violating ambassadors is just, but refers it to the people, who instead ELECT the Fabii to supreme office — influence and wealth defeating ius gentium; proximate political cause of the march on Rome.

quote: that Camillus should be recalled from exile at the comitia curiata, and be forthwith appointed dictator by order of the people
notes: The soldiery at Veii refuses to act without lawful appointment; a messenger swims through the siege lines so the rump senate can authorize recall and dictatorship — legality maintained in catastrophe (Livy underlines it). Camillus later annuls the gold ransom as concluded without the dictator's authority (5:49).

quote: beyond all the evils of siege and war, famine distressed both armies
notes: Starvation (not assault) forces the capitulation decision: senate instructs tribunes to treat; 1,000 pounds of gold agreed; false weights and 'Woe to the vanquished'; annulled by Camillus's arrival (5:49).

quote: that Marcus Furius, the dictator, should establish a college for that purpose, out of those who should inhabit the Capitol and citadel
notes: Post-sack religious reconstruction package: temples restored, Caere hospitality, Capitoline games with a new college, temple to Aius Locutius; matrons honored with funeral orations for their gold contribution.

quote: the tribunes were teasing the commons by their unceasing harangues, to leave the ruins, to remove to Veii, a city ready prepared for them
notes: Renewed migration-to-Veii agitation after the burning of the city; Camillus's speech (5:51-54) and the centurion's omen ('Standard-bearer, fix your standard!') decide it; law rejected and rebuilding begins with public tile subsidy (5:55). Camillus retains the dictatorship at the senate's request for this fight.

quote: a day of trial was named by Caius Marcius, tribune of the people, for Quintus Fabius, as soon as he went out of office
notes: Fabius prosecuted for fighting the Gauls while ambassador, contrary to the law of nations; he died before trial, a death widely thought voluntary.

quote: they ordered that the treaties and laws which could be found, should be collected
notes: Post-sack restoration: Twelve Tables and regal laws recollected, religious laws kept secret by pontiffs; dies Alliensis instituted as a black day.

quote: it was resolved that the state should be defended under the same auspices, as those under which it had been recovered, and that Marcus Furius should be nominated dictator
notes: Dictatorship against Volscians, Etruscans, and defecting Latins/Hernicians immediately after the Gallic sack.

quote: Four tribes were added from the new citizens, the Stellatine, the Tormentine, the Sabatine, and the Arnian
notes: Tribal structure expanded to twenty-five after enfranchisement of defectors from Veii, Capena and Falerii (admission and land grant narrated in 6:4).

quote: the tribunes of the commons endeavoured to draw crowds to their harangues by [proposing] the agrarian laws
notes: First Pomptine land agitation; little effect because the commons were absorbed and drained by rebuilding the city.

quote: Regarding the Pomptine land the matter was pressed by Lucius Sicinius, plebeian tribune, on the people, who now attended in greater numbers
notes: Renewed Pomptine agitation with growing attendance, deferred by the Etrurian war scare.

quote: and not content with agrarian laws, which had ever served the tribunes of the commons as material for disturbances, he now began to undermine public credit
notes: Manlius, first patrician to turn plebeian partisan, politicizes the immense rebuilding debt; start of the sedition spanning 6:11-6:20.

quote: But it was rather the reforming plans that drove the senate to create a dictator.
notes: Volscian war the colourable pretext; Livy says the real motive was Manlius's reform agitation.

quote: he ran up with his attendants in the middle of the forum and laid hands on him
notes: Manlius forcibly frees a condemned debtor, pays the debt publicly, sells his Veientian farm for debtors, and alleges concealed Gallic gold; crowd devotes itself to him.

quote: when he refused to speak, to meet the wishes of his enemies, he ordered him to be carried off to prison
notes: Dictatorial summons and imprisonment (confrontation staged in 6:15); Livy stresses that no one dared oppose legitimate dictatorial authority.

quote: decreed that a colony of two thousand Roman citizens should be conducted to Satricum; two acres and half of land were assigned to each
notes: Unsolicited senatorial largesse to appease sedition over Manlius; seen by the commons as a bribe and resented as scanty, irritating the sedition.

quote: The crowd did not disperse from that place even during the night, and they threatened that they would break open the prison
notes: Threat of prison-break conceded preemptively: Manlius released by senate decree, which Livy says supplied the sedition a leader rather than ending it; crowd invokes Cassius and Maelius precedents.

quote: Having summoned the commons to his house, he holds consultations both by night and day with the leading men amongst them with respect to effecting a revolution of affairs
notes: House assemblies aiming (Livy says, while noting no clear account survives) at regal power; calls for dictatorships and consulships to be levelled.

quote: that the magistrates should see that the commonwealth received no detriment from the designs of Marcus Manlius
notes: Early form of the ultimate decree, chosen over violence; tribunes of the commons side with the senate and devise prosecution through the people instead.

quote: The tribunes cast him down from the Tarpeian rock: and the same place in the case of one man became a monument of distinguished glory and of extreme punishment.
notes: Trial for aspiring to regal power; venue moved to the Poeteline grove out of sight of the Capitol to secure conviction; memorial sanctions follow (house razed, ban on the praenomen Marcus in the Manlian family); some authors said duumvirs condemned him.

quote: The pestilence was succeeded by a scarcity of the fruits of the earth
notes: Pestilence (which many read as divine anger at Manlius's execution, 6:20) followed by crop scarcity; army kept home on account of pestilence.

quote: they appointed five commissioners for distributing the Pomptine land, and three for conducting a colony to Nepete
notes: Distribution commission and colony explicitly granted to make the commons more disposed to vote for war against Lanuvium.

quote: neither the tribunes suffered those consigned to their creditors to be thrown into prison, nor did the young men give in their names
notes: Combined debt-enforcement blockade and levy refusal; tribunes also charge that wars are sought out deliberately to wear down the commons; broken only by the Praenestine advance on the walls (6:28).

quote: the matter having been commenced was interrupted by the death of Postumius, because it was not conformable to religion that a substitute should be colleague to a censor
notes: Censorship convened to ascertain the debt; successive appointments fail and tribunes allege the senate shuns the public tablets to hide the debt's scale.

quote: at length turning from sedition to war, they created Titus Quinctius Cincinnatus dictator
notes: Appointed in the panic of the Praenestine advance to the Colline gate; the terror of the office makes the enemy withdraw and the young men submit to enrollment.

quote: During the same year new colonists were enrolled for Setia, the colony itself complaining of the paucity of men.
notes: Reinforcement of an existing colony rather than a new foundation.

quote: the tribunitian power became even more vehement in obstructing the levy; until these conditions were imposed on the patricians, that no one was to pay tribute as long as the war lasted
notes: Levy released only after wartime suspension of tribute and of money judgments — an explicit institutional bargain; censors appointed to ascertain the debt were prevented by the war.

quote: legal proceedings began to be instituted anew; and so remote was all hope of relieving the former debt, that a new one was now contracted by a tax for building a wall of hewn stone
notes: New stone-wall tax stacked on old debt; with no levy to obstruct, the commons are forced to submit and even elect all-patrician military tribunes.

quote: they satisfied their creditors by their character and persons, and punishment was substituted for payment
notes: Debt bondage at its deepest point; plebeian political spirit so broken that no plebeian seeks even plebeian magistracies; the Fabia anecdote launching the Licinian program follows in the same chapter.

quote: the other concerning the limitation of land, that no one should possess more than five hundred acres of land
notes: The three Licinian-Sextian rogations: debt relief by deducting paid interest with three-year instalments, the 500-iugera land cap, and one consul necessarily plebeian — land, money and honours contested together.

quote: this total absence of magistrates continued in the city for the space of five years, the people re-electing the two tribunes, and these preventing the election of military tribunes
notes: Patricians procure colleagues' vetoes against the bills; Sextius and Licinius retaliate by vetoing curule elections — five years of solitudo magistratuum.

quote: It is resolved that a dictator be appointed: Marcus Furius Camillus is appointed, who nominates Lucius Aemilius his master of the horse.
notes: Dictatorship deployed against the rogations; Camillus sends lictors to disperse the voting commons, threatens a mass levy, then abdicates (defective auspices or the threatened 500,000-as fine); Publius Manlius substituted.

quote: Publius Manlius, dictator, then inclined the advantage to the side of the people, by naming Caius Licinius from the commons, who had been military tribune, as master of the horse.
notes: First plebeian master of the horse — read at the time as an omen for a plebeian consul; patricians displeased.

quote: For they passed the bills regarding the interest and the land, rejected the one regarding the plebeian consulate.
notes: The commons split the package; the tribunes force a collective vote on all three laws and stake their re-election on it, turning dissimulated refusal into leverage.

quote: succeeded in passing a law, that of the decemvirs for religious matters, one half should be elected from the commons
notes: Duumviri sacris faciundis replaced by decemviri, five plebeian — breaching the religious monopoly Appius Claudius had defended (6:41) and opening the way to the consulship.

quote: at which Lucius Sextius was made consul, the first of plebeian rank
notes: Licinian laws finally carried over dictator and senate; patrician refusal of ratification brought matters near a secession before Camillus brokered the compromise.

quote: with respect to one praetor to be elected out of the patricians, to administer justice in the city
notes: The compensating concession in Camillus's settlement; patrician curule aediles for the augmented games created in the same bargain.

quote: the sudden rumour of a Gallic war being brought, influenced the state to appoint Marcus Furius dictator for the fifth time
notes: Victory near Alba; Livy dates the Manlius-and-the-Gaul duel ten years later against Claudius's account — a source-criticism aside.

quote: remarkable for two new magistracies, the praetorship and curule aedileship. These honours the patricians claimed to themselves
notes: Praetorship and curule aedileship created as patrician compensation for conceding one consulship to the plebeians; curule aedileship soon agreed to alternate with plebeians every second year.

quote: The commons gave the consulship to Lucius Sextius, by whose law it had been obtained.
notes: First plebeian consul takes office under the Licinian law; patricians respond with obstruction (justitium-like inaction) and tribunes protest the three new patrician magistracies.

quote: the senate ordered a dictator to be appointed for the purpose of driving the nail. Lucius Manlius Imperiosus being appointed, named Lucius Pinarius master of the horse
notes: Dictator appointed for the religious rite of driving the nail to avert pestilence; Manlius then overreached by attempting to run the Hernician war.

quote: harassed the youth by a severe levy, and at length, all the plebeian tribunes having risen up against him, whether overcome by force or shame, he resigned the dictatorship
notes: United tribunician resistance to the nail-dictator's severe levy forces his resignation.

quote: a day of trial is appointed for Manlius, by Marcus Pomponius, tribune of the commons
notes: Tribunician prosecution for levy cruelty and abuse of his son; aborted in ch. 5 when the son Titus Manlius forced the tribune at dagger-point to swear off the prosecution — coercive (extraordinary) resolution the commons nevertheless tolerated.

quote: it had been determined on that year for the first time that tribunes of the soldiers for the legions should be appointed by suffrage
notes: Election of military tribunes transferred from commanders to popular suffrage; Titus Manlius wins second place of six on the episode's notoriety.

quote: the consul Servilius appoints dictator by the general wish of the patricians, and a levy and cessation of business are procaimed
notes: After the plebeian consul Genucius fell in ambush, patricians exulted and appointed Appius Claudius (opponent of the Licinian law) dictator; politically charged use of the office.

quote: It is sufficiently ascertained that Titus Quinctius Pennus was dictator that year, and that Servius Cornelius Maluginensis was his master of the horse
notes: Livy weighs variant traditions: Licinius Macer says appointed to block a consul's re-election ambitions, older annals say for the Gallic war; Livy prefers the latter and distrusts Macer's family bias.

quote: the alarm created by the Gauls rendered it necessary that a dictator should be appointed. Quintus Servilius Ahala having been appointed, named Titus Quinctius master of the horse
notes: Gallic return from Campania; battle at the Colline gate; dictator resigns after yielding triumph honours to the consuls.

quote: It was determined that Caius Sulpicius should be appointed dictator.
notes: Appointed against the Gauls at Praeneste/Pedum; his delaying strategy triggers the camp agitation coded separately.

quote: a disturbance just arising between the patricians and commons was checked by the dread of a war so near them
notes: Incipient domestic disturbance suppressed by the Tiburtine night attack; Livy gives no detail of its content.

quote: that they would either fight without the general's orders, or would proceed in a body to Rome
notes: Near-mutiny against the dictator's delaying strategy, voiced through chief centurion Sextus Tullius (chs. 12-14); defused when the dictator accepts battle — grievance accommodated rather than punished.

quote: a proposition was then for the first time made to the people regarding bribery at elections by Caius Paetilius, tribune of the commons
notes: First electoral-bribery (ambitus) law, carried with senate approval; aimed at the canvassing of novi homines in markets and meeting-places.

quote: by Marcus Duilius and Lucius Maenius, tribunes of the commons, regarding the interest of money at twelve per cent., and the people received and passed it with much more eagerness
notes: Tribunician law capping interest (fenus unciarium), displeasing to the patricians; part of the book's running debt-relief sequence.

quote: he passed a law regarding the twentieth part of the value of those set free by manumission
notes: Five-per-cent manumission tax voted by an assembly of tribes held irregularly in camp at Sutrium; senate sanctioned it for the revenue.

quote: passed a law, making it a capital offence for any one in future to summon an assembly of the people at a distance from the city
notes: Tribunician counter-law to the Sutrium precedent, fearing soldiers under military oath could be made to vote anything away from Rome.

quote: Caius Licinius Stolo was condemned in a fine of ten thousand asses, on his own law, by Marcus Popillius Laenas
notes: Author of the agrarian holding-cap convicted under it for possessing 1,000 iugera jointly with his emancipated son — the canonical enforcement-evasion anecdote for the Licinian land law.

quote: Caius Marcius Rutilus, being appointed dictator, the first plebeian who was so, named Caius Plautius, also a plebeian, master of the horse
notes: Patricians obstruct all decrees and preparations for his Etruscan war; he triumphs by order of the people without senate sanction — office and honour both won against patrician resistance.

quote: In the second interregnum a dispute arose, because two patrician consuls were elected: and the tribunes protesting
notes: Interrex Fabius answers tribunician protest with the Twelve Tables maxim that the people's latest order is law; tribunes only delay, two patricians elected in breach of the Licinian law.

quote: the commons followed in sorrow the tribunes, exclaiming, that there was an end of liberty; that not only the Campus should be relinquished, but the city also
notes: After days of blocked meetings the commons abandon the Campus Martius; consuls complete the election with the rump and again return two patricians.

quote: the poor were overwhelmed by the principal alone, and submitted to confinement
notes: Interest cap proves insufficient: principal still forces debtors into bondage (nexum-type confinement); private distress diverts the commons from contesting patrician monopoly of elections.

quote: ordered him to nominate a dictator. He nominated Titus Manlius, son of Lucius. He, after he had appointed Aulus Cornelius Cossus his master of the horse
notes: Appointed for the Caerite war; war declared by order of the people with senate sanction; resolved by Caerite embassy and hundred-year truce (ch. 20).

quote: the tribunes refusing to allow the elections to be held, unless they were held conformably to the Licinian law
notes: Elections blocked through eleven interreges; patricians finally order the interrex to observe the Licinian law and a plebeian consul (Marcius Rutilus) is returned for concord's sake.

quote: made the payment of the debts a matter of public concern, five commissioners having been appointed, whom from their management of the money they called bankers
notes: Quinqueviri mensarii: treasury pays off sound debts from tables of money in the forum or frees debtors by fair-price valuation of property — a state-funded debt workout Livy praises as clearing immense debt without complaint.

quote: rendered it necessary that a dictator should be appointed. Caius Julius was nominated in the camp
notes: Appointed on a groundless rumour that the twelve Etruscan states had conspired; then used politically (see ch. 22) to attempt a patrician-only consular election.

quote: An attempt made at home by the dictator, to have the election of two patrician consuls, brought the government to an interregnum
notes: The interreges achieve what the dictator could not: both consuls patrician, the people being mollified by the recent debt relief.

quote: Caius Marcius Rutilus, who had been the first plebeian dictator, having declared himself a candidate for the censorship, disturbed the harmony of the different orders
